LO 1 - Breath sounds by location

Auscultation

Expected Sounds vs Unexpected Sounds

The exam point is not just naming a sound. It is deciding whether that sound belongs in the place where you hear it. Bronchial or tracheal-quality sounds are normal near large airways; hearing them over peripheral lung fields should make you think about altered sound transmission through consolidated or tumor-infiltrated lung.

Key distinction

Air-filled lung muffles transmitted sound. Solid or fluid-filled alveoli can conduct sound more clearly, while air or fluid in the pleural space separates lung from chest wall and decreases transmission.

Lecture slide 39 - Bronchial sounds where vesicular sounds should be can suggest disease.

Lecture slide 29 - Lobe localization is approximate, especially laterally.

Normal Breath Sounds

SoundExpected LocationAcoustic PatternIf Heard Unexpectedly
VesicularMost peripheral lung fieldsSoft, low-pitched; inspiration longer than expiration; no gapNormal when symmetric and over lung parenchyma
Bronchovesicular1st-2nd interspaces anteriorly and between scapulae posteriorlyIntermediate pitch; inspiration about equal to expirationCan be abnormal if it replaces vesicular sound in distal fields
BronchialOver manubrium and large central bronchiLouder, higher-pitched; expiration longer than inspiration; brief pausePeripheral bronchial sounds suggest consolidation or mass effect
TrachealDirectly over tracheaVery loud, harsh, high-pitchedNot expected in peripheral fields; think abnormal transmission if heard away from central airway

Adventitious Sounds

SoundWhat You HearMechanismClinical AssociationsLocation/Timing Clue
CracklesDiscontinuous popping; fine or coarseAirways or parenchyma opening through fluid, exudate, or abnormal tissuePneumonia, CHF pulmonary edema, atelectasis, fibrosisFine late inspiratory crackles that persist suggest abnormal lung tissue; CHF crackles are often posterior/inferior

Exam Q

A patient with fever and productive cough has bronchial breath sounds at the right posterior base, where vesicular sounds are expected. What disease pattern does this support?

Right lower lobe consolidation, classically pneumonia. Solidified lung transmits central airway sounds better, so bronchial-quality sounds appear in a peripheral location.

LO 2 - Comprehensive pulmonary exam

Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation

A Practical Pulmonary Exam Workflow

The pulmonary exam follows the history. You are usually testing a hypothesis from symptoms, acuity, and risk factors rather than screening asymptomatic lungs for hidden disease.

Acuity first

Before the formal exam, decide whether the patient needs immediate help. Red flags include pallor, abnormal respiratory rate, central cyanosis of lips/tongue/mucosa, confusion, accessory muscle use, inability to speak full sentences, tripod positioning, or stridor.

Lecture slide 11 - Inspection can reveal barrel chest, deformity, asymmetry, or flail movement.

Lecture slide 27 - Compare side-to-side at matched levels; avoid diagonal laddering.

  1. Set up professionally. Hand hygiene, introduction, consent, comfort, bed height, and draping. Untie or move clothing only after asking permission; listen on skin, not through clothing.
  2. Inspect from the doorway and at bedside. Respiratory rate, rhythm, depth, effort, speech, color, mental status, posture, chest shape, symmetric expansion, retractions, nasal flaring, tracheal position, edema/capillary refill when relevant.
  3. Palpate. Chest wall tenderness, tracheal position at the sternal notch, chest expansion, tactile fremitus, and symmetry. A trachea deviating away can occur with tension pneumothorax; deviation toward can occur with volume loss such as atelectasis.
  4. Percuss. Use a side-to-side ladder on anterior, lateral, and posterior chest. Resonance is normal. Dullness, flatness, hyperresonance, or tympany should be interpreted in the clinical context.
  5. Auscultate. Ask the patient to breathe through an open mouth. Listen through a full respiratory cycle at each point, compare symmetric areas, and characterize intensity, pitch, timing, location, and change after cough or position change.
  6. Add special tests when indicated. Use transmitted voice sounds and excursions when you suspect consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax, obstruction, or asymmetric movement.

Percussion Notes

Lecture slide 26 - The five percussion notes to recognize.

Fast percussion interpretation

  • Resonant: normal air-filled lung.
  • Dull/flat: fluid or solid tissue replacing air or occupying pleural space, such as pneumonia, effusion, hemothorax, empyema, fibrosis, or tumor.
  • Hyperresonant: excess air, such as COPD/asthma; unilateral hyperresonance suggests pneumothorax or a large bulla.
  • Tympanic: gastric bubble normally; can occur with very air-filled cavities or pneumothorax.
Exam PartNormal FindingAbnormal FindingAssociated Processes
InspectionComfortable, full sentences, symmetric chest movement, no retractionsAccessory muscle use, nasal flaring, retractions, barrel chest, flail segment, cyanosisAsthma/COPD exacerbation, respiratory fatigue, COPD hyperinflation, trauma, hypoxemia
PalpationTrachea midline, symmetric expansion, symmetric fremitusTracheal shift, tenderness, asymmetric expansion, increased/decreased fremitusTension pneumothorax, atelectasis, consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax, obstruction
PercussionResonant and symmetric over lung fieldsDullness/flatness or hyperresonanceDull: pneumonia/effusion/mass. Hyperresonant: COPD/asthma/pneumothorax
AuscultationVesicular peripheral sounds without added soundsCrackles, wheezes, rhonchi, absent/distant sounds, bronchial sounds in peripheryCHF, pneumonia, asthma/COPD, secretions, pneumothorax/effusion, consolidation
Documentation pattern

Normal example: thorax symmetric with good excursion; lungs resonant; breath sounds vesicular with no added sounds; diaphragms descend about 4 cm bilaterally. COPD example: increased AP diameter, decreased expansion, hyperresonance, distant breath sounds, delayed expiratory phase, scattered expiratory wheezes, decreased fremitus, no egophony or whispered pectoriloquy, reduced diaphragmatic descent.

Exam Q

During posterior auscultation, why should you compare left and right at the same horizontal level rather than moving diagonally down the back?

The opposite side is the patient's internal control. Diagonal laddering compares different anatomic levels and can miss unilateral asymmetry.

LO 3 - Specialized pulmonary tests

Fremitus, voice sounds, excursions

Special Tests and What They Mean

Special tests are best used to answer a focused question: is sound being transmitted too well through solid lung, or too poorly because air/fluid/obstruction separates lung from chest wall?

Lecture slide 20 - Posterior respiratory expansion and tactile fremitus hand placement.

Sound transmission rule

Pneumonia and some lung masses act like a bullhorn if there is lung/tumor tissue to transmit vibration. Pleural effusion and pneumothorax usually reduce breath and voice sounds over the affected area because there is little or no aerated lung under the stethoscope.

TestHow To PerformNormalAbnormalDisease Associations
Tactile fremitusUlnar hands or palms on symmetric chest points while patient says "99" or "1-1-1" in a normal voiceSymmetric palpable vibrationIncreased, decreased, or asymmetric vibrationIncreased: consolidation/pneumonia, tumor-infiltrated lung. Decreased: pleural effusion, pneumothorax, obstruction, neoplasm with effusion or lung displaced from chest wall
Whispered pectoriloquyPatient whispers "99" or "1-2-3" while you auscultate in a ladder patternMuffled, indistinct, effectively absentWords become louder, clearer, or more distinctConsolidation or mass; decreased/absent over pleural effusion or pneumothorax
BronchophonyPatient says "99" out loud in normal voice while you auscultateMuffled, indistinct voice transmissionLouder, clearer spoken voiceConsolidation or mass that improves transmission
EgophonyPatient says "E" or "key"; listen over symmetric pointsE sounds like E or key sounds like key, often muffledE sounds like A, or key becomes kay-likeConsolidation/pneumonia or tumor-infiltrated lung; absent sounds suggest effusion or pneumothorax
Respiratory excursionHands around lower posterior ribs with thumbs near midline; patient inhales deeplyThumbs separate symmetricallyOne side lags or moves lessPneumonia, effusion, phrenic nerve paralysis, pulmonary fibrosis, bronchial obstruction, pneumothorax
Diaphragmatic excursionPercuss posteriorly to find diaphragm level at full exhale and full inhale; compare sidesAbout 3-5 cm by Bates; some sources use 4-6 cmLess than 3 cm or marked asymmetryPneumonia/parapneumonic effusion, COPD hyperinflation, phrenic nerve dysfunction, pleural disease

Increased transmission

Think solid lung: pneumonia, consolidation, tumor-infiltrated parenchyma. Findings cluster as increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, whispered pectoriloquy, bronchophony, and egophony.

Decreased transmission

Think separation from lung: pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or obstruction. Findings cluster as decreased breath sounds, decreased fremitus, and absent/decreased transmitted voice sounds.

Exam Q

A febrile patient with cough has dullness to percussion at the right base plus increased tactile fremitus and E-to-A egophony there. What is the most likely physical diagnosis?

Right lower lobe consolidation, most likely pneumonia. Dullness plus increased voice/vibration transmission points to solidified lung, not pleural air or pleural fluid.

LO 2/3 - Abnormal findings by disease

Pattern recognition

Disease Patterns From Exam Clusters

Most pulmonary exam questions are pattern-recognition questions. No single finding carries the whole case; the diagnosis comes from the cluster.

ProcessInspection/PalpationPercussionAuscultation/Special TestsHigh-Yield Clue
Pneumonia / consolidationMay have fever, tachypnea, asymmetric expansion; fremitus often increasedDull over affected regionBronchial breath sounds in periphery, crackles, egophony, bronchophony, whispered pectoriloquySolid lung conducts sound: "bullhorn" effect
Pleural effusionReduced expansion on affected side; fremitus decreasedDull or flat at base/effusion levelDecreased or absent breath sounds and transmitted voice over fluidNo lung in the fluid; CHF history can point toward effusion
PneumothoraxSudden dyspnea/pleuritic pain; decreased expansion; fremitus decreased; tension may shift trachea awayHyperresonant on affected sideDecreased or absent breath sounds; voice sounds decreasedUnilateral hyperresonance plus absent breath sounds
COPD / emphysemaBarrel chest, increased AP diameter, decreased expansion, possible accessory muscle useDiffuse hyperresonanceDistant breath sounds, prolonged expiratory phase, scattered expiratory wheezes, decreased fremitus, reduced diaphragm descentChronic smoking + progressive dyspnea + hyperinflation
Asthma / pulmonary obstructionTachypnea, accessory muscles, inability to speak full sentences in severe attacksMay be hyperresonant if air trappingDiffuse wheezes and prolonged expiration; silent chest is ominousWheeze means narrowed airways; absence of wheeze can be worse if air movement is minimal
CHF pulmonary edemaDyspnea, possible edema/JVD; central cyanosis if severeOften resonant unless effusion presentBilateral dependent inspiratory crackles; no egophony or increased fremitus in uncomplicated edemaBasilar crackles without consolidation signs
Lung massWeight loss, fatigue, hemoptysis; trachea may be midlineMay be normal or equivocal if deepFocal rhonchi from partial obstruction; egophony/whispered pectoriloquy if tumor-infiltrated tissue conducts soundCan increase or decrease fremitus depending on tumor vs associated effusion/obstruction
Pulmonary embolismPleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia; risk factors such as OCPs, immobilization, DVTOften normal/resonantOften nonspecific; no classic egophony or increased fremitusNormal-ish lung exam does not rule out PE
Pleural effusion nuance

The lecture emphasized: you need lung to hear breath or vocal sounds. Over fluid, breath and voice sounds should be decreased or absent. In some clinical teaching outside this deck, egophony can be heard at the upper border of an effusion where compressed lung sits above the fluid; do not call egophony "over the fluid" itself.

Consolidation

  • Dullness to percussion
  • Increased fremitus
  • Bronchial sounds where vesicular expected
  • Positive whispered pectoriloquy/bronchophony/egophony

Effusion or pneumothorax

  • Decreased breath sounds
  • Decreased fremitus
  • Decreased transmitted voice sounds
  • Dull if fluid; hyperresonant if air
Exam Q

A patient has decreased breath sounds at the left base, dullness to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus, and no egophony. Which is more likely: pneumonia or pleural effusion?

Pleural effusion. Pneumonia/consolidation usually increases voice/vibration transmission; fluid in the pleural space decreases it.

LO 4 - USPSTF pulmonary prevention

Preventive screening

USPSTF Rules You Should Apply in Vignettes

The course deck teaches the 50-80-20-15 lung cancer screening rule. I verified the USPSTF recommendation pages on 2026-08-17 and kept the notes aligned with the current USPSTF language.

Lecture slide 42 - Annual LDCT screening with the 50-80-20-15 rule.

Screening vs diagnostic testing

Low-dose CT is for screening eligible asymptomatic high-risk patients. If the patient has symptoms such as hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, focal findings, or concerning cough, the next test is diagnostic evaluation, not a screening LDCT.

TopicWhoUSPSTF ActionStop/AvoidVignette Hook
Lung cancer screeningAdults 50-80 with at least 20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 yearsAnnual low-dose CT; Grade BStop once quit time exceeds 15 years or if health substantially limits life expectancy or ability/willingness for curative lung surgery50-80-20-15. Age 81 is too old; age 45 is too young; quit more than 15 years ago is out.
Tobacco cessationAdults 18 or older, including pregnant personsAsk all adults about tobacco use. For nonpregnant adults who use tobacco, provide behavioral interventions and pharmacotherapy. For pregnant persons who use tobacco, provide behavioral interventions. Grade AEvidence is insufficient for pharmacotherapy in pregnant persons and for e-cigarettes as cessation tools; direct patients to proven interventionsDo it all the time and every time, especially if referring for LDCT screening.
COPD screeningAsymptomatic adults who do not recognize or report respiratory symptomsDo not screen asymptomatic adults for COPD; Grade DThis recommendation does not apply to symptomatic patients with cough, sputum, dyspnea, or wheeze, or to very high-risk groups such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or certain occupational exposuresNo spirometry screening just because the patient smoked if they have no symptoms; evaluate if symptomatic.
Exam Q

Which patient should receive annual LDCT lung cancer screening: (A) 65-year-old, 40 pack-years, quit 20 years ago; (B) 75-year-old, 50 pack-years, quit 10 years ago; (C) 81-year-old current smoker with 60 pack-years; (D) 45-year-old current smoker with 70 pack-years?

B. The patient is age 50-80, has at least 20 pack-years, and quit within 15 years. A quit too long ago; C is older than 80; D is younger than 50.

Exam Q

A patient with dyspnea has normal fremitus, normal percussion, no egophony, no crackles, and tachycardia after a long flight. Should you be reassured by the mostly normal lung exam?

No. Pulmonary embolism can have nonspecific or near-normal lung findings. The history and vital signs should drive diagnostic evaluation.

Week 4 Pulmonary - High-Yield One-Pager

1. Normal breath sounds by location

  • Vesicular: soft, low-pitched, inspiration longer than expiration, no gap - expected over most peripheral lung fields; this is the default sound.
  • Bronchovesicular: intermediate pitch/intensity, inspiration about equal to expiration - expected at the 1st-2nd interspaces anteriorly and between the scapulae posteriorly, over the mainstem bronchi.
  • Bronchial (tubular): loud, high-pitched, expiration longer than inspiration with a brief pause - expected only over the manubrium/trachea and large central airways.
  • Tracheal: loudest and harshest of all - normal only directly over the trachea.
  • Rule of thumb: sound should soften as you move from central airways toward the periphery; anywhere that sounds "too loud/tubular" for its location is a clue, not a variant.

2. Sounds in the wrong place

  • Bronchial or bronchovesicular quality heard over peripheral lung, where vesicular is expected, means abnormal sound transmission through solidified lung - think pneumonia, lobar consolidation, or tumor-infiltrated tissue.
  • Mechanism: air-filled alveoli normally filter out higher frequencies; fluid- or cell-filled (consolidated) alveoli conduct central-airway sound more efficiently out to the chest wall.
  • Vesicular sounds that are diminished, distant, or absent where they should be present mean something is blocking transmission - pleural air (pneumothorax), pleural fluid (effusion), or airway obstruction (mucus plug, mass, foreign body).
  • Always compare the same level side-to-side; asymmetry, not the sound in isolation, is what flags pathology.
  • Absent breath sounds plus unilateral hyperresonance plus trachea deviated away from that side = tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise.

3. Crackles (rales): fine vs coarse

  • Discontinuous popping sounds from collapsed airways/alveoli snapping open, or fluid/secretions bubbling.
  • Fine crackles: high-pitched, brief, late-inspiratory, "Velcro"-like - classic for pulmonary fibrosis/interstitial lung disease and early or mild CHF pulmonary edema.
  • Coarse crackles: lower-pitched, longer, louder, early inspiratory or biphasic - classic for pneumonia, bronchiectasis, and heavy secretions.
  • Crackles that clear with cough usually reflect secretions/atelectasis; crackles that persist after cough favor fibrosis, consolidation, or true pulmonary edema.
  • CHF crackles are classically bilateral, symmetric, and dependent (posterior/basilar bases).

4. Wheezes, rhonchi & pleural rub

  • Wheezes: continuous, musical, high-pitched - turbulent airflow through narrowed airways; hallmark of asthma and COPD/bronchospasm.
  • Expiratory-only wheeze suggests mild-moderate obstruction; wheeze on both inspiration and expiration suggests more severe narrowing.
  • A "silent chest" in an asthma exacerbation (no wheeze, minimal air movement) is a red flag for impending respiratory failure, not reassurance.
  • Rhonchi: low-pitched, snoring/gurgling - from secretions or partial obstruction in larger airways (bronchitis, mucus plugging); often clears or shifts after coughing.
  • Focal rhonchi that persist after cough should raise concern for an obstructing lesion or mass, not simple secretions.
  • Pleural rub: coarse, grating, leathery, heard on both inspiration and expiration - inflamed pleura (pleuritis, pneumonia near the pleura, PE); usually localized and painful with breathing.

5. Inspection

  • Look before you touch: respiratory rate/rhythm/depth/effort, symmetry of chest wall movement, accessory muscle use (SCM, scalenes), nasal flaring, retractions (supraclavicular, intercostal, subcostal).
  • Chest shape: barrel chest/increased AP diameter signals chronic air trapping (COPD/emphysema).
  • Color: central cyanosis (lips, tongue, mucosa) means significant hypoxemia; peripheral cyanosis can just reflect poor circulation.
  • Clubbing of the digits: chronic hypoxemia from lung cancer, bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis, or cystic fibrosis.
  • Tripod positioning, inability to complete full sentences, or stridor signals impending respiratory failure - act before finishing the formal exam.

6. Palpation & percussion

  • Palpation: tracheal position at the sternal notch (should be midline), symmetric chest expansion (thumbs at the costal margin), tactile fremitus, focal tenderness.
  • Trachea deviates away from a tension pneumothorax (pushed by pressure); deviates toward volume loss such as atelectasis or lobar collapse.
  • Percussion: side-to-side ladder pattern comparing matched levels - never march diagonally down the back.
  • Resonant = normal aerated lung. Dull/flat = fluid or solid tissue replacing air (pneumonia, effusion, hemothorax, empyema, fibrosis, tumor).
  • Hyperresonant = excess air - diffuse in COPD/asthma, unilateral in pneumothorax or a large bulla. Tympanic is expected only over the gastric bubble.

7. Auscultation technique & tactile fremitus

  • Listen on bare skin, diaphragm of the stethoscope, patient breathing deeply through an open mouth, full respiratory cycle at each point, compare side-to-side.
  • Characterize every sound by pitch, intensity, timing (inspiratory/expiratory/both), location, and whether it changes with cough or position.
  • Tactile fremitus: palpate symmetric points with the ulnar edges/palms while the patient says "99" or "1-1-1" in a normal voice.
  • Increased fremitus = consolidation/pneumonia or tumor-infiltrated lung transmitting vibration well.
  • Decreased/absent fremitus = pleural effusion, pneumothorax, obstruction, or COPD hyperinflation - anything separating lung from chest wall or reducing airflow.

8. Voice sounds & excursion

  • Egophony: patient says "E"; normal is a muffled "E." Over consolidation the sound changes to a nasal "A" (E-to-A change) - same mechanism as increased fremitus.
  • Bronchophony: spoken "99" becomes louder and clearer over consolidation (normally muffled).
  • Whispered pectoriloquy: whispered "1-2-3" becomes loud and distinct over consolidation (normally inaudible/indistinct) - the most specific voice test for consolidation.
  • All three voice tests are decreased or absent over effusion or pneumothorax, since there is no aerated or solid lung to transmit sound.
  • Diaphragmatic excursion: percuss to find the diaphragm level at full exhale vs full inhale; normal is about 3-5 cm and should be symmetric. Decreased/asymmetric excursion occurs with COPD hyperinflation, large effusion, phrenic nerve paralysis, or pulmonary fibrosis.
  • Respiratory (chest wall) excursion: hands on the lower posterior ribs with thumbs meeting at midline - asymmetric separation localizes the side of disease (pneumonia, effusion, pneumothorax, fibrosis, bronchial obstruction).

9. Consolidation vs effusion vs pneumothorax

  • Pneumonia/consolidation, "solid lung transmits sound": dull to percussion, increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds where vesicular is expected, crackles, positive egophony/bronchophony/whispered pectoriloquy.
  • Pleural effusion, "fluid blocks sound": dull-to-flat percussion, decreased fremitus, decreased/absent breath and voice sounds, decreased chest expansion on that side.
  • Pneumothorax, "air blocks sound and there is no lung to hear": hyperresonant percussion, decreased fremitus, decreased/absent breath and voice sounds; the tension variant shifts the trachea away from the affected side.
  • Quick discriminator: effusion and pneumothorax both look "quiet" (everything decreased) - tell them apart with percussion: dull/flat means fluid, hyperresonant means air.
  • Pneumonia is the "loud" pattern (increased transmission); effusion/pneumothorax are the "quiet" patterns (decreased transmission) - this pairing is the single most tested concept in this unit.

10. COPD, asthma & CHF patterns

  • COPD/emphysema: barrel chest, decreased expansion, diffuse hyperresonance, distant/decreased breath sounds, prolonged expiratory phase, decreased fremitus, reduced diaphragmatic excursion - chronic smoking history.
  • Asthma/obstruction: accessory muscle use, possible hyperresonance from air trapping, diffuse wheezing with prolonged expiration; a silent chest in a severe attack is a crisis, not improvement.
  • CHF/pulmonary edema: bilateral dependent (basilar) inspiratory crackles, percussion usually resonant unless a co-existing effusion is present, no egophony and no increased fremitus - this is not a consolidation pattern.
  • CHF vs pneumonia: CHF crackles are bilateral, symmetric, and basilar with a normal voice-sound exam; pneumonia crackles are typically more focal/unilateral with positive egophony and increased fremitus.

11. USPSTF: lung cancer screening & tobacco cessation

  • Lung cancer screening, Grade B: annual low-dose CT for adults age 50-80 with at least a 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years - the "50-80-20-15" rule.
  • Stop screening once the patient has not smoked for more than 15 years, or if a health problem substantially limits life expectancy or the ability/willingness to undergo curative lung surgery.
  • LDCT is a screening test for asymptomatic high-risk patients; a patient with hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, or a worrisome focal finding needs diagnostic workup, not a screening order.
  • Tobacco use and cessation counseling, Grade A: ask every adult, including pregnant patients, about tobacco use at every visit.
  • For non-pregnant adults who use tobacco, offer both behavioral counseling and pharmacotherapy; for pregnant patients, offer behavioral counseling (pharmacotherapy evidence is insufficient in pregnancy, as is evidence for e-cigarettes as a cessation tool).

12. USPSTF: COPD screening & vignette traps

  • COPD screening, Grade D: USPSTF recommends against screening asymptomatic adults for COPD - no routine spirometry just because someone has a smoking history but no symptoms.
  • This Grade D recommendation does not apply to patients who already have respiratory symptoms (cough, sputum, dyspnea, wheeze) - evaluate those patients rather than withholding testing.
  • It also does not apply to special high-risk groups, such as known alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or significant occupational/environmental lung exposure.
  • Classic exam trap: an asymptomatic ex-smoker asking for a "lung function check" - correct answer is no spirometry screening, but do assess tobacco use and lung-cancer-screening eligibility.
  • Grade pattern to memorize: lung cancer screening is FOR (Grade B), tobacco cessation counseling is FOR everyone (Grade A), COPD screening in asymptomatic adults is AGAINST (Grade D).
